paras: The Lorain mob attack on Charles Hall and Robert Pleasant took place on the night of 28 July 1903 in Lorain, Ohio, when a crowd of about 300 white men chased two Black men through the south end of the city, threatening to lynch them. The crowd stoned a saloon where one of the men hid and fired shots, but no one was killed; Pleasant was jailed and the mayor persuaded the mob to disperse. Because one wire copy carried a Lawrence, Massachusetts dateline, some southern papers treated the episode as proof that lynching had reached New England.

Early in the evening, shortly after seven o'clock according to the Cleveland Gazette, the two men got into an argument with a white man, Daniel Cronan, in a saloon, and a fight followed. One of the two men was reported to have drawn a razor and cut Cronan on the face and neck.

As news of the cutting spread, a mob formed and chased the men over the south end of the city. One of them took refuge in a saloon, which the Gazette said was owned by Robert Fountain, and the crowd threw stones and clubs at it, battering in its front and "breaking almost every pane of glass in the house." The man nonetheless escaped.

The city's entire day and night police force was ordered on duty and special policemen were sworn in. Late that night, at nine o'clock in the Gazette's account, police arrested Pleasant and took him by side streets to the station, while the crowd kept searching and fired a number of shots. Around ten o'clock Mayor King met the crowd at Ninth street, told it that Cronan's injuries were not serious, and urged it to go home and "let the law take its place," after which the mob dispersed.

Pleasant was placed under a $100 bond and held in the city jail, and a later digest reported that Cronan would recover. No report of a hearing or trial, or of any arrest among the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The story went out as a wire dispatch datelined Lorain, appearing on 29 July in the Indianapolis Journal under the headline "Chased by a White Mob" and the same day in the Salt Lake Herald. The New-York Tribune ran it under "Ohio Falls Into Line," casting it as part of the spread of mob violence through the old Northwest, and the Atlanta Constitution printed it on 3 August as "Ohio Mob After Negroes," with the crowd put at 500. Versions differed on the first man's name, printed both as Charles Hall and as Charles Hill.

The Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas printed the same text under a "Lawrence, Mass." dateline, with 400 whites and a "Charles Pleasant." Southern papers seized on that version: the Americus Times-Recorder remarked that the mob was now "trying to lynch negroes in Massachusetts," and on 24 August the Brownsville Daily Herald reprinted a Mexican Herald editorial, under a slur headline, mocking the abolitionist state.

The Black press reported the episode as a lynching averted. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed the wire under "Stop Lynchings," pairing it with a Wheeling, West Virginia case and crediting police in both towns with preventing mobs "from Taking Vengeance." The Cleveland Gazette gave its own fuller account under "The Mob Dispersed," calling the crowd "300 lawbreakers" and attributing the trouble in its subhead to "West Virginia Residents of Lorain."

The Lawrence dateline, the 400 figure and the name Charles Pleasant appear only in the Bryan copy and the editorials that followed it, while the earliest wire copy and the Gazette's separate report place the event in Lorain and name Robert Pleasant. The Brownsville editorial dated the riot to "the 26th ultimo," against the 28 July date given by the dispatches.

reader.title: Lorain mob attack on Charles Hall and Robert Pleasant
bases: A white mob of about 300 chased two Black men 'threatening to lynch them', stoned the saloon where one took refuge and fired shots before the mayor dispersed it; no one was killed (A1, A6, A9).

A mob of some 300 whites pursued the two men under the pretext of punishing the razor cutting of Daniel Cronan, but no one was killed, so it does not meet the standard definition; the papers describe a threatened or attempted lynching (A1, A6, A9).

The Associated Press-style Lorain wire (A1, A4, A5) and the Cleveland Gazette's separately written account with its own details on times, the saloon owner and Pleasant's bond (A6) agree on the core events.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 whites chased two colored men after one cut Cronan with a razor, battered a saloon front with stones, and fired shots; Pleasant was arrested and the mayor dispersed the crowd.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette account
accounts.gist: A crowd of '300 lawbreakers' formed after a saloon argument and fight shortly after 7 p.m.; the man fled into Robert Fountain's saloon, which was stoned and clubbed; Pleasant was arrested at 9 and bonded at $100; the mayor spoke at 10.

accounts.label: Lawrence, Mass. misdateline
accounts.gist: The same wire text appeared datelined Lawrence, Mass., with 400 whites and 'Charles Pleasant', and was taken up by southern editorials as a Massachusetts event.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headed the wire 'Chased by a White Mob' and 'Two Negroes Pursued by Crowd of Would-Be Lynchers', crediting the mayor with ending it.
The New-York Tribune ran it as 'Ohio Falls Into Line', treating it as part of a spread of mob violence to the old Northwest.
Southern editorials mocked Massachusetts and its abolitionist past, the Brownsville Herald's reprint under a slur headline, on the strength of the Lawrence misdateline.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate headed the wire 'Stop Lynchings' and praised police for preventing mobs 'from Taking Vengeance'.
The Cleveland Gazette called the crowd '300 lawbreakers' and blamed 'West Virginia Residents of Lorain' in its subhead.

conflicts.note: The Lawrence version carries the same wire text, including 'Ninth street' and the mayor; the Lorain dateline is in the earliest copy and in the Cleveland Gazette's separate account, so Lorain is the better evidence.
The 26th appears only in a derivative editorial weeks later; the 'June 28' in the Atlanta copy contradicts its own July publication and is a misprint.
Robert Pleasant is printed in all Lorain versions; Hall and Hill both appear, including in the Black press.
Most copies, including the Gazette's separate account, say 300.

'The negro' who took refuge escaped; Pleasant arrested
